summary: Defines a framework for standardizing metrics of bulk transport capacity, which is how much data a single congestion-controlled connection can move. It aims to cover the variety of transport behaviors.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3148 explains how to define measurements of the data rate a single congestion-aware connection can achieve. It asks each method to state its exact rules and collect supporting information so readers can compare results and understand differences.

questions: how is bulk transfer capacity defined
subtitle: A framework for making measurements of bulk data transfer capacity comparable.

tldr.problem: Bulk Transport Capacity (BTC) measures the long-term data rate of one congestion-aware connection, but permitted transport choices can make results from different tools incomparable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what data counts in the rate and requires each BTC method to specify its transport behavior closely. It also recommends collecting supporting measurements about the path and the test platform.
tldr.outcome: This is a framework for defining BTC metrics, not a metric or measurement tool. The RFC says the framework may need revision as congestion-control work develops.

today: RFC 3148 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the text says the framework may need revisiting as congestion-control work develops.

sections.title: What Bulk Transport Capacity Measures
sections.content:
Bulk Transport Capacity (BTC) is the long-term average rate at which one congestion-aware transport connection transfers a large amount of data over a network path. The RFC defines the reported value as data_sent / elapsed_time.

data_sent counts unique data bits, not header bits. If data is retransmitted, it is counted once. The framework is intended to help define comparable BTC metrics; it does not define one particular measurement method.
sections.plainLanguage: BTC measures how quickly one connection transfers a large amount of data over a path. The count includes each data bit once, but excludes the bits used for headers.

sections.title: Why Each Metric Needs Precise Rules
sections.content:
TCP standards allow implementers choices in congestion control. Different choices can produce results that cannot be compared directly, so a BTC method needs to specify important implementation details more closely than a typical protocol document.

The RFC also notes that performance may not rise smoothly as path capacity changes. New congestion-control algorithms and work on Explicit Congestion Notification could affect measurements, so the framework may need to be revisited.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tests can report different rates because they use different rules for responding to congestion. Each BTC method must spell out those rules so readers know what its result means.

sections.title: Transport Behavior a Method Must Specify
sections.content:
BTC implementations MUST use slow start and congestion avoidance as specified in RFC 2581, and MUST implement a retransmission timeout. They SHOULD implement fast retransmit and fast recovery.

Each BTC method MUST state which congestion-avoidance algorithm it uses, what it does when the congestion window equals the slow-start threshold, and how any advanced loss-recovery method works. It must also define segment size, assumed header bytes, retransmission-timeout calculation, clock setting, and clock granularity.
sections.plainLanguage: A BTC method must describe how its connection increases its sending rate and responds when data is lost. It must also specify packet size and the timer rules used to decide when to retransmit.

sections.title: Measurements That Explain the Result
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that each method collect ancillary metrics, or enough information to derive them later, such as a trace of transmitted segments. These measurements help compare results with analytical models and investigate why two methods differ.

Examples include Congestion Avoidance Capacity, loss of the acknowledgment clock, packet reordering, congestion-window size, packets dropped inside the sending host, and queue lengths at that host. A method should also report relevant reverse-path load and whether advanced TCP features are needed to match the measured capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: The rate alone may not explain a test result. Information about losses, packet order, and limits inside the sending computer can help show what affected the measurement.

sections.title: Security and the Framework's Limits
sections.content:
This framework does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security. A test built from it may fill a bottleneck link and could look like a denial-of-service attack, especially if it does not use TCP packets. The RFC says the involved network administrators may agree on the timing, size, and frequency of tests.

The tests generate packets rather than sampling user data, so the RFC says they do not threaten user-data confidentiality. It notes that interference with test packets could distort results and that cryptographic hashes may help detect such interference. The document has no IANA considerations for the framework itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A BTC test can use enough capacity to worry network operators, so they may need to agree when and how it runs. The RFC also notes that tampering with test packets can distort a result.
